title: Sokółka’s Far-Flung Community: Aid and Remembrance Beyond the Town
summary: The landsmanshaftn and descendants’ activities show how ties to Sokółka continued through aid, commemoration, and the preservation of the memorial book.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Organization of Sokolka Emigrants in Israel

editorialContent:
![Sokółka, the town remembered by its emigrants and survivors](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ed/Jarmark_%E2%80%93_ko%C5%84_-_Sok%C3%B3%C5%82ka_-_000723s_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)

## A community carried beyond its streets

The Jewish community of Sokółka did not end at the town’s borders. Long before the Holocaust, people left for Palestine and the United States, carrying with them memories, friendships and ties of mutual assistance. After the destruction of the community, those connections became a way to help survivors and keep Sokółka present in places far from northeastern Poland.

The memorial book, published in Jerusalem in 1968, presents that work as a shared undertaking. Its editors were survivors and emigrants who assembled testimony, photographs and names to make a memorial for people whose graves were often unknown. It also acknowledges Sokółka Jews in America who supported the book’s associated charitable work. The memorial book is a community’s act of remembrance, not a complete register of everyone who left, survived or was lost.

The record identifies an [Organization of Sokolka Emigrants in Israel](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_2d6ee8d41605d5713c0538b8) and a separate [Sokolka Organization in Israel](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_84e6e01eeb5de79f0c484ed6). These names may refer to related or overlapping bodies, but the supplied evidence does not establish that they were identical. The book’s printed Hebrew organization name is also difficult to recover with certainty from the OCR. What is clear is the purpose: Sokółka’s survivors and emigrants organized themselves around a town that could no longer sustain its former communal life.

## Committee members and the work of rebuilding ties

The Israel organization’s recorded members include [Yudovsky](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_8fe2ce7b7797dd2e14a570ea), [Reiskind](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_7d9f56e086d4491dc3024eb6), [Tikatsinsky](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_c4212d616a32506403afdf2e), [Bonim](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_ea7e593d104ba645cdd2c58f), [Shapiro](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_42fa148fae037a40fe430f53), [Even](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_aaa48ad2b5456686ac64d237), [Studnik](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_ff27e79e9e8bd1f9f413eb91), [Hasid](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_0550f6439f4b2e148c4446ba) and [Manasevich](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_f279287e7177067d6db823e0). The record names these people, but provides little biographical detail; names alone do not establish family relationships or individual wartime fates.

The memorial book’s broader account places this organizing in a longer history of Sokółka’s Zionist life and emigration. Some residents had left for Palestine before the war. In a recollection about visiting Sokółka in 1933, one emigrant describes having made a life in Palestine while remaining attached to the town of his birth. That sort of earlier migration meant that postwar connections were not created from nothing: they extended networks formed across decades. But the organization’s exact founding date and activities beyond those represented in the book remain uncertain.

## New York: fundraising and practical solidarity

Across the Atlantic, the [Sokółka Jewish Society](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_11e46b51389e94679278cfcf) operated in New York. The memorial-book evidence links it to fundraising for projects in Israel and to campaigns for the United Jewish Appeal. Its officers included [Meir Kaplan](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_6db39739b62aed9e08e37cec), listed as president; [Ida Pazarnik](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_a2c6881510408d87551f5231), vice president; [Jack Epstein](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_93d08f9974d636178f02f3ee), recording secretary; and [Molly Epstein](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_648b3edd4b42448b731153da), corresponding secretary.

The book’s foreword describes a more specific form of support: American Sokółka refugees helped sustain a fund called *G’milat-Tsedek*, a benevolent loan fund associated with the martyrs of Sokółka and the surrounding area. According to the book, it assisted members who sought help, including Holocaust survivors and new immigrants to Israel. This was remembrance expressed through practical care—not only commemoration, but lending and mutual aid.

These New York activities should not be collapsed into the Israeli organization’s work. The sources show people and institutions on both sides of the ocean, linked by origin and concern for Sokółka, but they do not give a full organizational chart or prove that all bodies operated as one association. The society’s local records, including its fundraising accounts and correspondence, remain a promising [research question](research:What New York records document the Sokółka Jewish Society, its leaders, and its aid to survivors?).

## The memorial book as a meeting place

The most durable shared project was the memorial book itself. Published in Jerusalem in 1968, *Sefer Sokolkah* gathered community history, personal recollections, accounts of destruction, lists of names and material about Sokółka emigrants in Israel and America. The book’s preface says that survivors approached people in Israel and the Diaspora for memories because few records of everyday communal life had survived. It describes the volume as a memorial for parents, siblings, friends and neighbors, as well as an attempt to prevent the names of the murdered from disappearing.

That editorial project was also a meeting point between generations. Its dedication to American town-fellows and its sections on emigrants show that readers outside Israel were part of the intended audience. The book’s [list of Sokółka emigrants in Israel](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_5ddb3757f9160b09be496c2a) is one trace of the community dispersed across borders; like any list assembled for a memorial volume, it should not be mistaken for a complete census.

The book also preserves a short statement about an [annual remembrance gathering](/communities/sokolka/records/event_candidate_c05ee4b68d3b719883aecc23): “We, the sons of Sokółka, gather every year and mourn.” The words capture a recurring act of communal mourning, but the supplied excerpt does not specify where the gathering took place, when it began, or who attended. Its very brevity conveys something important: descendants and survivors made remembering a collective practice, not just a printed one.

## What outside records add—and what remains open

Yad Vashem’s *Encyclopedia of the Ghettos* supplies essential historical context, but does not document these diaspora organizations. It estimates that about 2,800 Jews lived in Sokółka at the outbreak of war and describes the town’s Jewish political, educational and charitable institutions. It also records the German occupation, the establishment of the ghetto and deportations through Kielbasin, with most residents deported onward to Treblinka in late 1942. The entry dates the deportation of most remaining ghetto residents to Auschwitz-Birkenau to February 23, 1943. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=691&utm_source=openai))

That chronology differs from David Yardeni’s memorial-book account, which says Sokółka’s Jews were gathered in the town square on January 18, 1943, and taken on their “last journey.” These accounts may describe different stages or groups in the liquidation, but the available evidence does not resolve the discrepancy; it should not be turned into a single, falsely precise date. The Yad Vashem entry confirms the scale and sequence of persecution while also showing why the book’s testimony and the later historical reference must be read distinctly.

A Wikipedia entry on Sokółka independently summarizes the destruction and notes that the Jewish community was not re-established after the war. It also mentions commemoration by former Jewish residents and people from surrounding villages, though it is not a substitute for archival evidence about the specific organizations or their members. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sok%C3%B3%C5%82ka?utm_source=openai)) No independent source found here verifies the named committee members, New York officers, annual gathering or aid fund. Those details remain grounded in the memorial book and its extracted records.

The story that emerges is therefore both substantial and incomplete. Sokółka’s emigrants and survivors organized across Israel and New York, raised funds, supported one another and made a book intended to carry the destroyed community into the future. Yet the surviving names and summaries leave many questions: who belonged to more than one organization, how the annual gathering was maintained, and what became of relatives absent from the memorial lists. Those unanswered questions are part of the history too: the book preserved much, but no single memorial could hold the whole dispersed community.
